deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is the final page of Riemann's 1857 memoir 'Zwei allgemeine Lehrsätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten'. The page continues with the editor H. Weber's footnote and the start of the fragment printed after it in the Werke (1876).

(1) End of the degenerate-case remark from the previous page. If the monodromy cannot be kept constant while a moves, the system is a special case of a system with lower exponents. For those special positions of a,…,g, the leading coefficients of some of the local series (α)^{-1}(y), (β)^{-1}(y), … vanish.

(2) Isomonodromic-deformation statement. Consequence of the theorem: y_1,…,y_n are functions of p variables a,b,…,g,x. Let these variables run around any closed path in their joint space and return to their old values. Then the vector (y_i) returns either to itself or to a linear transform Y ↦ M·Y with constant M. M is composed from the p−2 arbitrarily prescribed substitution matrices (A),(B),…,(F).
- In modern terms: if the singular points move while the monodromy representation is held fixed, the fundamental solution extends to a (multivalued) function of (a,…,g,x).
- The monodromy of this extended function in the deformation variables is generated by the original monodromy matrices.

Riemann declines to pursue this further. He remarks on two things:
- An abelian integral (the integral of an algebraic function) is a special case: n=2, with solutions 1 and ∫R dx.
- Applying these principles to such integrals leads to functions representing the general θ-series with arbitrary period moduli. Here 'arbitrary' means not restricted to the period matrices of Jacobians.

(3) Weber's footnote, to be set as a note under the text.
- Riemann's fair copy carries the marginal remark 'von hier an nicht richtig' where the final part begins.
- Weber printed that part anyway, because it may contain the germ of a further theory.
- He then reproduces, from draft sheets, 'die Grundzüge zu einer Weiterführung' of the investigation.

(4) Fragment 'Bestimmung der Form der Differentialgleichung'. The task is to find the simplest systems of each class and determine the form of their ODE.
- Now let y', y'', …, y^{(n)} denote successive derivatives, in Lagrange's notation. Then equations (2) become the n-th order linear ODE satisfied by the y_i.
- To find the degrees of its polynomial coefficients: each x-differentiation lowers every local exponent by 1, provided none is an integer.
- Hence at x=a the Wronskian W = det(y_j^{(i-1)}) has exponent Σ_i μ_i − n(n−1)/2 =: μ̄, and likewise ν̄,…,ς̄ at b,…,g.
- Therefore X_0 := W·(x−a)^{-μ̄}(x−b)^{-ν̄}…(x−g)^{-ς̄} is finite and single-valued everywhere, i.e. a polynomial. The monodromy multiplies W by det M, which cancels against the factors.
- The page breaks off here.

Continuation on the next page:
- At ∞ (an ordinary point) W ~ x^{-n(n-1)}.
- So deg X_0 = r = (m−2)·n(n−1)/2 − s, where m is the number of finite branch points and s = Σ μ̄ + n(n−1)/2 summed appropriately, i.e. the sum of all characteristic exponents.
- Since r ≥ 0 counts apparent singularities, this is the Fuchs relation. [Explicit infinity bookkeeping mine.]
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.
The differentiation rule (each exponent drops by exactly 1) correctly carries the stated proviso that no exponent is an integer.
The isomonodromy claim is asserted without proof. Riemann himself marked the preceding final section 'von hier an nicht richtig' (reported by Weber).

The degenerate case (insufficient free constants to keep the monodromy fixed) is only sketched. The modern theory needs genericity or irreducibility hypotheses and must handle the Riemann–Hilbert obstruction and the Malgrange divisor.

results.what: Solutions of a Fuchsian system with fixed monodromy, viewed as functions of the singular points a,…,g and x, have monodromy in all variables generated by the given substitutions
Abelian integrals as a special case; the method leads to general theta series with arbitrary period moduli
results.modern_name: Theta functions from isomonodromy / Schottky-type considerations; Riemann–Hilbert approach to theta functions

results.what: The Wronskian times ∏(x−a_k)^{-μ̄_k}, with μ̄_k = Σμ − n(n−1)/2, is a polynomial X_0 (the leading coefficient of the ODE)
results.modern_name: Wronskian local exponent / construction of the Fuchsian equation from monodromy data

results.what: Degree count leading to r = (m−2)n(n−1)/2 − s (on the next page)
results.modern_name: Fuchs relation (with r = number of apparent singularities)

deep.surprise_reason: This page is the published end of Riemann's 1857 memoir plus the fragment printed by Weber in the Werke (1876). Riemann's anticipation of isomonodromic deformations and of the Fuchs relation is well documented in the literature (Gray, Bottazzini, Its, and others).

checkable.asserts: The Wronskian exponent at a point equals the sum of the exponents minus n(n−1)/2, for n=2 (result 0).
At a regular point at ∞, W ~ x^{-n(n-1)} for n=3 (result 0).
The degree formula r=(m−2)n(n−1)/2−s gives r=0 for the Papperitz/Riemann P-equation with 3 finite singular points and ∞ ordinary (exponent sum 1), so there are no apparent singularities.
Differentiation lowers the local exponent μ by one (μ non-integer).

transcription_corrections: Line 1–2: 'α^Γ(y), β^Γ(y) … δ^Γ(y)' should read (α)^{-1}(y), (β)^{-1}(y), …, (ϑ)^{-1}(y), matching the notation of the previous page.
In the Wronskian formula the exponents rendered 'Γ, ∇, ς' are μ̄, ν̄, …, ς̄ (overlined Greek letters) and are positive in the factors: (x−a)^{-μ̄}(x−b)^{-ν̄}…(x−g)^{-ς̄}.
'derivirten [?] zusammengesetzt' is doubtful; the printed Werke text reads simply '…Systemen (A), (B), …, (F) zusammengesetzt ist' (the word may be 'beziehungsweise' or similar).

The Weber footnote begins roughly 'Die Handschrift weist eine vollständig ausgearbeitete Reinschrift nach[?]'. The inserted word above the struck one is likely 'Ueberlegungen'/'eingeklammerten' (uncertain).
'die n Differentialgleichung' should read 'die Differentialgleichung n-ter Ordnung'.
'Σ ± (y_1 y_2' … y_n^{(n−1)})' denotes the Wronskian determinant.
